title: Earth
def: The Quran describes the earth as spread out as a resting place for people; classical Muslim scholars knew it to be round.
what: The Quran says God “spread out” the earth (dahāhā, 79:30; madda, 13:3), made it a resting place (2:22) and set mountains on it as stabilisers (16:15). It also speaks of the night wrapping or coiling around the day (39:5). These are descriptions as seen from the ground.
misread: That the Quran teaches a flat earth, or that it states the earth is egg-shaped.
sources: The word in 79:30 has been rendered “spread out”, and some translate it “egg-shaped” on the basis of a rarer meaning, which scholars do not generally accept. Medieval Muslim scholars knew the earth was a sphere: al-Biruni and the astronomers under the caliph al-Ma’mun measured its circumference in the ninth century, and Ibn Hazm argued from it. The Quran’s point in the verses is God’s provision.

title: Earthquakes
def: In the Quran earthquakes are among the signs by which earlier peoples were destroyed, and chapter 99 describes the final quake.
what: Thamud and Midian were seized by an earthquake (7:78, 7:91). Chapter 99, “The Earthquake”, describes the earth shaken and giving up its burdens on the Day of Judgement, when people see the results of what they did, “whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it” (99:7).

title: East and west
def: “To God belong the east and the west” (2:115): no direction contains God, though prayer faces the Kaaba.
what: “To God belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the face of God” (2:115). “Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is whoever believes in God and the Last Day…” (2:177). The Quran also speaks of “the Lord of the two easts and the two wests” (55:17), and “the Lord of the east and the west” (73:9).
sources: The two easts and two wests are read as the two points of sunrise and sunset in summer and winter. The direction of prayer was changed from Jerusalem to Mecca in the second year after the hijra (2:142–150), as the entry on the qibla explains.

title: Ebionites
def: An early Jewish-Christian sect that kept the Jewish law and held that Jesus was a man chosen by God; some writers compare their view to the Quran’s.
what: The Ebionites (“the poor”) are known mainly from Church writers such as Irenaeus and Epiphanius. They followed Jesus as the Messiah and kept the Torah, and some denied his virgin birth and divinity. They were later condemned as heretics.
misread: That the Quran’s account of Jesus comes from the Ebionites.
sources: Some scholars have proposed a link, and Muslims reject it. The Quran affirms the virgin birth (3:47, 19:20), which the Ebionites generally denied, and it does not describe Jesus as a Jewish sect’s teacher. Its portrait of Jesus is the Quran’s own, and Muslims hold that it comes from God.

title: Eclipse
def: The Prophet taught that the sun and moon eclipse by God’s decree and not for anyone’s birth or death, and prescribed a special prayer.
what: When the Prophet’s infant son Ibrahim died, an eclipse of the sun happened the same day, and people said it was for his death. The Prophet answered: “The sun and the moon do not eclipse for the death or life of anyone; they are two signs of God. When you see them, pray” (Sahih al-Bukhari).
sources: The hadith is cited as an example of the Prophet rejecting a superstition that would have favoured him, at a moment of grief. The eclipse prayer is a sunna of two long units.

title: Egypt
def: The land of Joseph and of Moses, whose stories the Quran tells at length.
what: Joseph rose in Egypt from a slave to a minister (12:21, 12:54–56), and later Moses faced Pharaoh there. The Quran names nine signs given to Moses (17:101), among them the flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood (7:133), and tells of the sea parting (26:63). Pharaoh’s pursuit ends with his drowning, and God says “today We will save your body, that you may be a sign for those after you” (10:92).

title: Ehrman, Bart
def: An American scholar of the New Testament (b. 1955), whose books on its manuscripts are often cited in Muslim-Christian argument.
what: Bart Ehrman was an evangelical Christian, and is now an agnostic. His Misquoting Jesus (2005) sets out how scribes changed the New Testament text in copying. Other scholars, including conservative Christians, say that he overstates the effect of the variants.
sources: Some Muslims quote him to support the view that the Gospels were altered. Careful Muslim writers note that he himself says most variants are trivial and that the reconstruction of the early text is secure in the main. His work shows that the history of the text is more complicated than either side sometimes assumes.

title: Eid
def: The two Muslim festivals: Eid al-Fitr, at the end of Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha, at the Hajj.
what: Eid al-Fitr falls on the first of Shawwal, and Eid al-Adha on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijja. Each begins with a congregational prayer in the morning, followed by a sermon. Fitr is preceded by zakāt al-fiṭr, a charity for the poor, and Adha recalls Abraham’s offering by the sacrifice of an animal, a third of which is given to the poor.
sources: Anas reports that when the Prophet came to Medina, the people had two days of play, and he said that God had given them two better days, the Eid of sacrifice and the Eid of breaking the fast (Abu Dawud).

title: Elijah
def: Elijah, a prophet of Israel who the Quran says called his people from Baal to God.
what: The Quran lists Elijah among the righteous (6:85) and tells of his call: “Do you invoke Baal and forsake the best of creators?” (37:123–126). He is praised: “peace upon Elijah” (37:130). A later passage speaks of “Ilyasin”, which some read as the same name.

title: Elisha
def: Elisha, a prophet named among the righteous (6:86, 38:48).
what: The Quran names him with Ishmael, Jonah and Lot among those “whom We favoured over the worlds” (6:86), and again among “the chosen and the best” (38:48). The stories of his miracles are not told in the Quran.

title: Embryology
def: The Quran describes human creation from clay and then a drop, a clinging substance, and a lump, in stages (23:12–14).
what: “We created man from an essence of clay; then We made him a drop in a firm resting place; then We made the drop a clinging clot, then the clot a lump, then made the lump bones, then clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation” (23:12–14; also 22:5, 75:37–39). The Prophet is reported to have said that the creation is assembled over forty days, and that an angel then breathes in the spirit (Sahih al-Bukhari).
misread: That the Quran gets embryology wrong, or that it predicted modern embryology.
sources: Muslim scholars disagree. Some argue that the stages correspond to modern ones, and cite a modern embryologist’s endorsement. Others say that the Quran’s description, given in simple terms, matches those found among earlier writers, such as Galen, and that its purpose is to show God’s power in creation and the certainty of resurrection. Critics point to “bones, then clothed with flesh”, which does not match the order of development, and defenders read the verb kasā as “covered”, as the muscles form around cartilage.

title: Enemies
def: The Quran tells believers to repel evil with good, to be just to enemies, and perhaps to turn enmity into friendship.
what: “Repel evil with what is better, and the one between whom and you is enmity will be as if he were a close friend” (41:34). “Do not let hatred of a people make you unjust; be just, that is closer to piety” (5:8). “Perhaps God will place affection between you and those whom you have held as enemies” (60:7). The Prophet, after he was stoned at Ta’if, was offered by the angel of the mountains to crush the town between two mountains. He refused, saying “perhaps God will bring from their descendants those who worship God alone” (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Environment
def: The Quran calls humans stewards (khalīfa) of the earth, forbids waste and corruption, and sets a balance (mīzān).
what: “Eat and drink, but do not be wasteful; He does not love the wasteful” (7:31, 6:141). “Do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set right” (7:56). “He raised the heaven and set up the balance, so do not transgress the balance” (55:7–8). The Prophet said that if the Hour is about to come and one of you has a sapling in his hand, he should plant it (Ahmad), and that any Muslim who plants a tree or sows a crop from which a bird, person or animal eats has given charity (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Envy
def: Envy, the wish that another lose what God has given him, is forbidden and condemned in the Quran (4:32, 113:5).
what: “Do not covet what God has bestowed on some of you over others” (4:32). Chapter 113 asks refuge “from the evil of an envier when he envies”. The Prophet said: “Do not envy one another, and do not hate one another” (Sahih al-Bukhari). He allowed envy only in a figure of speech, for two people: one who is given wealth and spends it rightly, and one who is given wisdom and teaches it (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Equality
def: The Quran teaches the equality of all people before God (49:13) and commands justice (4:135); the rules of classical law, however, did draw distinctions of status.
what: “O you who believe, stand firmly for justice, as witnesses for God, even against yourselves, or your parents and relatives” (4:135). The Quran says the noblest before God is the most pious (49:13). The Prophet said that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab except in piety. The Quran’s “law of retaliation” (2:178) sets equal penalty for killing.
misread: That Islam teaches the equality of all people in law, or that it teaches the inequality of some.
sources: Classical law made distinctions between free and slave, Muslim and non-Muslim, man and woman in some matters of inheritance, witness and retaliation. Muslim thinkers hold that the principle was equality before God and justice for all, and that the particular rules were shaped by their age, and many modern scholars and states have revised them.

title: Esposito, John L.
def: An American scholar of Islam at Georgetown University, a leading writer and commentator, whom some criticise and others admire.
what: John Esposito (b. 1940) is a Catholic scholar who founded the Center for Muslim-Christian Understanding at Georgetown. He has written widely on Islam and politics. His critics say he is too sympathetic to Islamist movements, and his supporters say he has sought to explain Muslims fairly.

title: Ethics and conduct
def: The Quran’s teaching on character, justice, honesty and kindness in everyday life.
what: “God commands justice and good conduct, and giving to relatives, and forbids indecency and wrongdoing and oppression” (16:90). “Be just; it is closer to piety” (5:8). “Do not follow what you have no knowledge of” (17:36). “Avoid much suspicion” (49:12). The Quran tells the Prophet: “you are of great character” (68:4). He said that he was sent to perfect good character (Ahmad).

title: Eusebius
def: Bishop of Caesarea (c. 260–340), author of the first history of the Church.
what: Eusebius wrote the Ecclesiastical History, which preserves many early Christian writings, and a Life of Constantine. He took part in the Council of Nicaea in 325. His history is a main source on early Christianity, and Muslim and Christian writers alike cite it.

title: Eve
def: Adam’s wife, who in the Quran shares Adam’s mistake and his repentance.
what: The Quran does not name her. It says God created people “from a single soul and created from it its mate” (4:1). In the story of the tree both Adam and his wife are tempted and both repent (7:19–23); in 20:121 the slip is Adam’s, and in 2:36 Satan caused both of them to slip. The Quran does not blame her alone.
misread: That Islam blames woman for the fall, or that she was made from a rib.
sources: A hadith says that “woman was created from a rib, so treat women kindly” (Sahih al-Bukhari). Many scholars read it as a figure of speech about women’s nature, not an account of Eve’s creation, and as advice on kindness. The Quran’s own account says nothing of a rib.

title: Evil
def: The Quran teaches that good and evil befall people as trials by God’s permission, and that a person is responsible for his own wrong.
what: “Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself” (4:79). “We test you with evil and with good as a trial” (21:35). The Quran also says “repel evil with what is better” (41:34, 13:22) and describes the reward of the patient (28:54).

title: Evil eye
def: Islamic tradition holds that envy can harm, and teaches protective prayers.
what: The Prophet said “the evil eye is real” (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim). The practice is to say “mā shāʾa Allāh” (what God wills) when admiring something, and to seek refuge by reciting the last two chapters of the Quran. In a report in the Muwaṭṭaʾ, Sahl ibn Hunayf fell ill after a man admired him, and the Prophet advised washing.
sources: Muslim scholars warn against amulets, and the Prophet said that whoever hangs an amulet has committed shirk (Ahmad). The remedy is to remember God.

title: Evolution
def: Muslims differ on evolution: many accept it for animals, and most hold that Adam was created directly.
what: The Quran says that God created people “in stages” (71:14) and “from clay” (38:71). Medieval writers such as al-Jahiz and Ibn Khaldun described a gradual ranking of living things, which some modern writers have called a forerunner. In recent times Muslim opinion has been divided: some accept evolution, some reject it, and some, like many Christians, accept it and hold that God guided it.
sources: Many scholars hold that the Quranic account of Adam as a distinct creation, an honoured one, is to be taken as it stands. Others point out that the Quran does not say how long the creation of people took.

title: Extremism
def: The Quran calls Muslims a “middle community” and forbids excess in religion; Muslim scholars have condemned terrorism.
what: “Thus We made you a middle community” (2:143). “People of the Book, do not go to excess in your religion” (4:171, 5:77). The Prophet said: “Beware of excess in religion; those before you were destroyed by excess” (Ahmad, al-Nasa’i) and “those who go to extremes are destroyed” (Sahih Muslim). He described a group who would recite the Quran but whom it would not benefit, a description the scholars later applied to the Kharijites.
sources: In 2004–05 the Amman Message, endorsed by hundreds of scholars from all schools, affirmed that no one may call another a non-Muslim, and rejected terrorism and killing in God’s name. The Prophet said that whoever kills a person under a treaty will not smell the fragrance of Paradise (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: Ezekiel
def: A prophet of Israel; some commentators link the Quran’s story of the thousands who left their homes and were revived (2:243) with his vision.
what: “Have you not considered those who left their homes, thousands, fearing death? God said to them ‘die’, then He gave them life” (2:243). Commentators such as al-Tabari relate it to the vision of the dry bones of Ezekiel, and say that Ezekiel prayed over them. The Quran does not name him here.

title: Ezra
def: The Quran says “the Jews say Uzayr is the son of God” (9:30); Muslim commentators relate this to a particular group.
what: “The Jews say: ‘Uzayr is the son of God’, and the Christians say: ‘the Messiah is the son of God’” (9:30). Commentators such as Ibn Abbas relate it to a few Jews of Medina and elsewhere in Arabia. Ezra the scribe is held in great honour in Judaism for restoring the Torah after the exile, and later Jewish writings exalt him.
misread: That the Quran makes an error about Jewish belief.
sources: The Quran does not say that all Jews held this, and the text says “the Jews say”, as the Bible uses “the Jews” for particular groups. No scholar claims Judaism teaches it, and Muslims do not. The matter is taken up in the article linked here.
